findings.location: sections/concise/10-commentary.tex L300-301, L309-310, L316 (The lifted soul and those who wait)
findings.problem: The rebuilt Psalm 24 unit opens 'The Introit's psalmist lifts his soul to God, and three of the authors take up from what and toward what it is lifted', and later says 'Gregory and Aquinas speak of where the soul goes'. Gregory says nothing of the psalmist's soul. Hom. in Ev. I.1.3 explains the Gospel's levate capita ('Levare itaque capita est mentes nostras ad gaudia patriae coelestis erigere'). The tie to the Introit is the first interpretation's, as the expansive study marks it (sections/20-lift-up-your-heads.tex L215-222: 'If that is the command, the psalmist in the Introit's first line is already doing what the Gospel asks'). The next clause ('Gregory, explaining the Gospel's leváte') and L311-313 restore the right attribution, so a careful reader is not misled, but the two framing sentences credit Gregory with a reading of the psalm that the study draws. The comparison itself is sound. Aquinas, Super Ps. 24 n. 1, has 'per erectionem mentis in Deum', which matches Gregory's 'mentes ... erigere' exactly; only the framing over-credits Gregory. Isolated instance.
findings.required_result: Make the framing true of each author, for example at L300-301: 'The Introit's psalmist lifts his soul to God, and the Gospel tells the disciples to lift their heads. Three authors say what the lifting is, and from what or toward what.' At L316: 'Gregory and Aquinas speak of where the mind is raised; Augustine, of what the soul leaves.' Keep L311-313, which marks the link between the psalmist and the Gospel's command as the first interpretation's.

findings.location: sections/concise/10-commentary.tex L403-421 (The Collect, the Secret and the Postcommunion, first paragraph)
findings.problem: The topic sentence 'The interpretations differ on where the cleansing from sin comes from' (L406-407) does not match what the paragraph shows. In all four interpretations the cleansing comes from the gifts the Secret names. The first and third set the Secret beside what Gregory and Paul tell the sinner to do, and L413-415 says they 'make the same contrast'; the second says what the cleansing removes, and the fourth what it prepares for. The sentence presents complementary uses as a disagreement, which the three-document profile forbids ('Neither smooth incompatible identifications into one account nor dramatize complementary emphases as a dispute'). Two smaller points in the same paragraph. First, 'the Secret asks the cleansing of the gifts themselves' (L411) can be read as asking that the gifts be cleansed; the expansive study has 'asks for the cleansing from the holy gifts themselves' (sections/20-lift-up-your-heads.tex L209-210). Second, the opening quotation of Schuster's paraphrase of the Collect (L403-405) restates a petition the themes pages already explain (04-themes.tex L57-59), and the parallel it seems to set up, 'by his power' beside the Secret's 'by their mighty power', is never drawn. The paragraph came from the repair of SYN-001 and SYN-003. Isolated instance.
findings.required_result: Replace the topic sentence with one the paragraph supports, for example: 'The interpretations set the Secret's cleansing beside different things: the first and third beside what Gregory and Paul tell the sinner to do, the second beside what the cleansing takes away, the fourth beside what it prepares for.' At L411 write 'and the Secret asks for the cleansing that the gifts themselves give.' Open the paragraph with the Secret ('The Secret asks the holy gifts to cleanse us poténti virtúte, by their mighty power.') and drop the Schuster sentence, since L408 already refers to 'the danger the Collect names'. Alternatively, keep the Schuster sentence and say in a clause what the two powers have to do with each other.

findings.location: sections/concise/10-commentary.tex L30-32; L222-225; L469-470 (against L378 and L386-387)
findings.problem: Three small defects. (a) L30-32: 'He counts what his hearers had seen, nation rising against nation, earthquakes, pestilence, and "fiery battle lines in the sky"'. Gregory (Hom. in Ev. I.1.1, tracked Wikisource passage) says that earthquakes overthrowing cities are heard of from other parts of the world ('ex aliis mundi partibus scitis quam frequenter audivimus') and that pestilences are suffered ('patimur'). Only the strife of nations and the fiery battle lines are 'seen' ('cernimus', 'vidimus'). The expansive study keeps this distinction (sections/20-lift-up-your-heads.tex L28-34). (b) L222-225: 'for "we ought to hasten to them as fast as we can" (I.1.3)'. Here 'them' has no antecedent in the concise. Gregory's 'ea' are 'coelestis patriae gaudia aeterna', the joys of the heavenly homeland, which the concise first mentions only at L302-303. (c) L469-470: the commentary's last sentence ('The fourth alone sets the two explanations of the Communion's earth against each other; the second and third read its fruit as good works without the dispute') repeats what the earth unit has just said at L378 and L386-387. Editorial.md, 'Say it once': a closing comparison compares; it does not re-argue each section.
findings.required_result: (a) For example: 'He counts what his hearers had seen or heard of: nation rising against nation, earthquakes reported from other lands, pestilence without end, and "fiery battle lines in the sky" before Italy fell to the sword of the heathen'. (b) For example: 'for, knowing the joys of the heavenly homeland, "we ought to hasten to them as fast as we can" (I.1.3)'. (c) Cut the last sentence, or replace it with a comparison the earth unit has not already made.

observations.location: generated/scriptural-date-location-page.tex via research/chronology-table.tex and research/chronology-annotations.tex: Alleluia row (Ps. 84:8), Communion row (Ps. 84:13), Introit row (Ps. 24:1--3, 24:4)
observations.note: First page-2 lookup: the passage Ps 84:8. The row 'Alleluia: Ps. 84:8 (Vg.; Heb. 85)' gives the Historical setting as 'Occasion date unresolved' and the Composition as 'The Psalms of the Sons of Korah, c. 740--536 B.C. (Korahite collection estimate)'. Passage and date are easy to pair, but no place is given, nor is the place marked unknown; the Communion row (Ps 84:13) is the same. Second lookup: Ps 24:1-3 (Introit) gives David's reign, Hebron then Jerusalem, c. 1055--1015 B.C. (usual chronology; Corbett also reports dates 30--50 years later), with composition before c. 165 B.C. Both lookups succeed for passage, occurrence and date. The missing place on the Korahite rows, like the Epistle row's noted at iteration 0, is a matter for the shared projection, not for this synthesis.

observations.location: sections/concise/10-commentary.tex L329-333; research/scope.md L152; research/interpretations.md L219; sections/30-coming-through-the-church.tex L206-211
observations.note: SYN-002(a) was resolved by verification rather than deletion. The registered Corpus Thomisticum response for Super Psalmos 21-30 (refetched, SHA-256 and byte size matching the artifact record) reads at Super Ps. 24 n. 4 'Per has enim vias venit dominus ad nos, maxime per praeceptum caritatis', so the concise now attributes the charity clause to Aquinas correctly. The research records quote n. 4 only as far as 'ad nos', and the expansive study gives the clause in its own voice ('by the commandments and above all the commandment of charity'). Both upstream owners could be aligned with the source when next touched.

No print edition was requested, so physical pagination was not judged. The opening blocks are in the established order, separated by clearpage. A plain count with LaTeX commands and comments removed gives about 1,550 words for the themes, 5,120 for the commentary and 940 for the apparatus, in agreement with the production record.

summary: Cold review of the concise study (synthesis.tex: sections/concise/01-inventory, 02-overview, generated page 2, 04-themes, 10-commentary, 90-apparatus) of the Claude 1962 First Sunday of Advent, iteration 1, read before the expansive study and then compared with it. The accepted expansive study is byte-identical to the inputs study review 3 sealed, and only 04-themes, 10-commentary and 90-apparatus changed since synthesis review 0. The three standing blocking findings are repaired. SYN-001: the Psalm 24, earth and orations units now set the authors side by side on a stated question (Gregory and Aquinas on the raising of the mind, Augustine on what the soul leaves, Aquinas and Bellarmine on the ways; Rupert and Bellarmine against Augustine on the fruit, with the other interpretations placed against both; one Postcommunion paragraph), and the announcing sentences are gone. SYN-002: the conditionals ('would then begin', 'would be one place'), Gregory's herald and judge in the closing comparison, and Aquinas's 'preparation for prayer' are restored; (a) is resolved by verification, because Super Ps. 24 n. 4 reads 'Per has enim vias venit dominus ad nos, maxime per praeceptum caritatis' in the registered Corpus Thomisticum response (refetched, SHA-256 5e8fdbbe...66ed and 271,127 bytes matching the artifact record). SYN-003: the seven repetitions of the themes pages are removed or reduced to brief back-references. Advisories SYN-004 to SYN-009 are cleared. Checked at source: Gregory, Hom. in Ev. I.1.1-4 (tracked Wikisource passage); Aquinas, Super Ps. 24 nn. 1 and 4 and Super Rom. 13 lect. 3 (Corpus Thomisticum responses refetched, both hashes matching); Augustine, En. in Ps. 24.1-3 and 24.10 (tracked NPNF passages); Bellarmine on Ps 24:1-4 (tracked O'Sullivan passages). From the concise prose alone each interpretation's answer can be recovered: real signs and a world not loved (Gregory, Cyril of Alexandria); the Church's lights and a coming already under way (Ambrose, Augustine); the sleeper told to rise and Christ asked to set him free (Chrysostom, Aquinas); Christ given as man and to be given as God (Augustine, Bellarmine). Page-2 lookups were made for Ps 84:8 and Ps 24:1-3 and both succeed (observations). Register is plain and nothing recurs at a level that should block. Three isolated advisories remain: a framing sentence that credits Gregory with the Introit's lifting (SYN-010), a Secret topic sentence that presents complementary uses as a disagreement (SYN-011), and three small wording defects (SYN-012). Limits: no print edition was requested, so pagination was not judged. Ambrose, Letter 199, Chrysostom and the two Cyrils were not refetched, because the concise only compresses quotations of theirs that the accepted study prints unchanged. Verdict: PASS.
